term_en: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
definition_en: The original inhabitants of the land that is now Australia — Aboriginal peoples of the mainland and Tasmania, and Torres Strait Islander peoples of the islands between Queensland and Papua New Guinea.
An independent national body that looks into complaints about discrimination and breaches of human rights; racism can be reported to it.
The departments of the Australian Government and the people who work in them — for example staff at Services Australia.
Large-scale public disorder such as demonstrations and riots, usually by people protesting against a government decision or policy.
Two or more political parties joining together, usually so they can form a government or an opposition when no single party has a majority.
A group of people given an official responsibility — for example, the independent commission that runs elections.
Australia's supreme law, which the government must follow; it sets out the legislative, executive and judicial powers.
A country whose head of state is a king or queen whose powers are limited by the Constitution. Australia is one.
The place where a judge or magistrate hears legal cases; people who break the law may be brought there.
A hearing in a court that examines the facts to decide whether a person is guilty or not guilty of a crime.
Using technology to threaten, intimidate, harass or humiliate someone with the aim of hurting them. Many forms are illegal and should be reported to the police and the online platform.
Government by the people, exercised through the representatives they elect to parliament.
Behaviour or threats used to control a partner by causing fear or endangering their safety. It is against the law and should be reported to the police.
Carrying or buying illegal drugs in order to sell them; a serious federal crime.
The process by which citizens choose the people who will represent them in parliament. Citizens aged 18 or over must vote.
The official list of people who are registered to vote in elections and referendums.
An area whose voters elect one member to the House of Representatives; also called an electoral district, division or seat.
To make sure people obey the law; this is what the police do when they keep the peace.
Having the same status as everyone else; Australians believe all people are equal.
The authority to administer and carry out the laws made by Parliament — held by ministers and the Governor-General. One of the three powers in the Constitution.
The idea that everyone, whatever their background, should have an equal chance to succeed in life.
The joining of separate colonies into one nation, with each former colony (now a state) keeping certain powers. Australia federated in 1901.
The eleven ships that sailed from Britain to set up a convict settlement in New South Wales, landing at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788.
A national or state flower; Australia's is the golden wattle.
A marriage in which one or both people did not freely agree to marry. It is illegal in Australia.
From now on and into the future — the opening words of the citizenship pledge.
A widely recognised image or landmark, such as the Sydney Opera House.
Relating to the Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples, the First Peoples of Australia.
The process by which migrants adapt so they can take part in, and contribute to, their new and changing society.
The authority to interpret and apply the laws, held by the courts. One of the three powers in the Constitution.
The authority to make and change the laws, held by Parliament. One of the three powers in the Constitution.
Personal freedom and independence — such as freedom of speech, expression, religion and association.
A judge who presides over a lower court.
Helping others and accepting their help, especially when times are hard.
A nation's official song; Australia's is 'Advance Australia Fair'.
A system of government in which citizens regularly elect representatives to parliament, and those representatives make the laws.
A group of people who share similar ideas about how the country should be governed and usually try to get elected to put those ideas into practice.
Prejudice, discrimination, harassment or hatred aimed at someone because of their race, colour, or national or ethnic origin. It is against the law.
A vote by all enrolled voters on a proposed change to the Australian Constitution.
Someone who acts or speaks on behalf of others, such as a member of parliament or a local councillor.
Showing consideration for another person, and for the decisions they make.
The principle that everyone — citizens, leaders and the government itself — is bound by the law, and nobody is above it.
The Australian Government agency that delivers health, social and welfare payments and services through Medicare, Centrelink and Child Support.
A way of voting in private so that no one can see your choice or pressure you about it.
Separate from religion. Australia's government is secular and there is no official national religion.
Able to provide for your own needs without relying on others, for example by having a job.
To establish, build or start something, such as a colony or an organisation.
A type of local government area, usually rural, run by a council.
Government pensions and benefits that support people in need, such as the unemployed, people with disability and older people.
The government agency that collects tax and manages the tax and superannuation systems that fund services for Australians.
The principles that guide a person in judging right from wrong and deciding how to act. Australia has a shared set called Australian values.
A person who freely gives their time to help a person or organisation without expecting to be paid.
